title: Transparent, translucent and opaque: why more layers let less light through

summary.text: One sheet of paper over a drawing still lets you see it, but a few sheets hide it. Even then, a torch still glows through the pile. Your child sorts home things into three kinds: transparent things we can see through, translucent things that let light through but no clear picture, and opaque things that block the light. Then they count how many layers of polythene, tissue and paper it takes to hide a drawing. They find that each layer stops some of the light, so how thick a thing is matters as much as what it is made of.
summary.art: A girl at a kitchen table laying white paper squares one by one over a drawing of a sun, with a pile of clear plastic squares and tissue squares beside her and a torch ready.

intro.hook: Hold one paper napkin up to a window, and light shines through it. Hold up a whole packet of napkins, and it looks dark. Where did the light go?
intro.text: Some things let light through, and some things block it. But the same paper can do both. One sheet glows in the light. A thick pile looks dark. In this unit you find out which things let light through, and you count how many layers it takes to stop it.
intro.art: A boy holding one paper napkin up to a bright window, glowing, and a girl beside him holding up a whole thick packet of napkins, dark.

outcomes: By the end I can say what transparent, translucent and opaque mean, and give a home example of each.
By the end I can sort things into the three kinds by holding them up to the light.
By the end I can show, by counting layers in a fair test, that more layers of a material let less light through.
By the end I can explain that a pile of paper can hide a picture and still let light through.
By the end I can say that a thin slice of almost anything lets some light through, and a thick enough piece of anything stops it.
By the end I can explain why the deep sea is dark, although a glass of water is clear.

terms.meaning: A transparent material lets light go straight through it. You can see clearly through it.
terms.example: Window glass, clean water and a clear polythene bag are transparent.
terms.art: A clear glass tumbler of water with a spoon and a smiling face drawn on a card behind it, both easy to see.

terms.meaning: A translucent material lets some light through, but you cannot see a clear picture through it. It glows when light is behind it.
terms.example: A paper napkin, a thin cotton dupatta and the skin of an onion are translucent.
terms.art: A paper napkin held up to a window, glowing white, with only a blurry patch where the window is.

terms.meaning: An opaque material does not let light through. You cannot see anything through it, and it does not glow.
terms.example: A steel plate, a wooden door and a brick wall are opaque.
terms.art: A steel plate held up to a bright window, with the plate dark and a bright edge of light around it.

terms.meaning: A layer is one sheet or one thickness of something. Layers can be piled on top of each other.
terms.example: Ten paper squares piled up make ten layers.
terms.art: Squares of white paper piled up like a little tower, with the number of layers written beside it: 1, 2, 3, 4.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of.
terms.example: A tumbler can be made of glass, steel or plastic. Those are three materials.
terms.art: Three tumblers in a row, one glass, one steel and one plastic, with a label under each.

terms.meaning: A fair test is a test where we change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then we know what made the difference.
terms.example: In the Layer Test, we change only the material. The drawing, the light and the size of the squares stay the same.
terms.art: Three piles of squares, polythene, tissue and paper, each on the same drawing of a sun, under the same window.

explanations.concept: Three ways a material can treat light
explanations.definition: A transparent material lets light go straight through. A translucent material lets some light through, but spreads it in all directions, so you see no clear picture. An opaque material lets no light through.
explanations.description: Remember the three plates, where you held things up to the window? Glass and clear plastic showed you the window clearly. They are transparent. A napkin and an onion skin glowed, but you could not see the window through them. They are translucent. A steel plate was dark, with no glow at all. It is opaque.
examples: Transparent: a glass tumbler, a clear polythene bag, clean water.
Translucent: a paper napkin, a dry onion skin, a thin cotton dupatta.
Opaque: a steel plate, a wooden spoon, a brick wall.
explanations.context: This card says what the three words mean.
explanations.art: Three panels: an arrow of light going straight through glass, an arrow breaking into many small arrows inside a napkin, and an arrow stopping at a steel plate.

explanations.concept: Each layer stops some of the light
explanations.definition: When light goes through a layer of a material, some of the light is stopped and the rest goes on. Each new layer stops some more. So many layers let through much less light than one.
explanations.description: Remember the Layer Test, where you piled squares on a drawing? One square of paper let you see the drawing. With every square you added, the drawing got fainter, until it was gone. Each layer sent some light back and soaked up some more. Only the rest went on to the next layer. Polythene stopped very little light, so the drawing still showed through many layers.
examples: In the Layer Test, the drawing got fainter with each paper square.
One napkin glows at a window, but a whole packet of napkins looks dark.
A thin cotton curtain lets light into a room. Two or three curtains, one behind the other, make the room much darker.
explanations.context: This card says why more layers let less light through.
explanations.art: Five paper squares in a row, with a fat arrow of light going into the first and the arrow getting thinner after each square.

explanations.concept: Hidden is not the same as dark
explanations.definition: A pile of translucent layers can hide a picture completely and still let light through.
explanations.description: In the Layer Test, a few paper squares hid your drawing. Then you shone a torch behind the same pile, and it glowed. So light was still getting through. Each layer spreads the light out a bit more, so the picture gets mixed up. After a few layers, no picture is left, but some light still comes out.
examples: The paper pile that hid the drawing still glowed with the torch behind it.
A closed bathroom window of frosted glass lets in daylight, but you cannot see out.
Your eyelids let in a red glow when you face a bright window, but you see no picture.
explanations.context: This card says why a pile can hide a picture but still glow.
explanations.art: A pile of paper squares on a drawing, the drawing hidden, and the same pile held over a torch in a dim room, glowing softly.

explanations.concept: Thin enough, almost anything lets light through
explanations.definition: A thin enough slice of almost any material lets some light through. A thick enough piece of any material stops nearly all light.
explanations.description: A whole cucumber is opaque. A paper-thin slice of the same cucumber glows at the window. Gold hammered into very thin gold leaf lets greenish light through, but a gold bangle does not. Scientists who study rocks grind them into slices thinner than paper, and most rocks then let light through. So whether something is opaque often depends on how thick it is.
examples: A thin cucumber slice glows. A thick piece looks dark.
Thin gold leaf lets green light through. A gold coin does not.
Rock ground thinner than paper lets light through, so scientists can study it under a microscope.
explanations.context: This card says why thin things let light through.
explanations.art: A whole cucumber, dark, next to a paper-thin cucumber slice held up to a window, glowing pale green.

explanations.concept: Why the deep sea is dark
explanations.definition: Water is transparent, but each metre of water stops a little light. Below about 1,000 metres, no sunlight reaches at all.
explanations.description: A glass of water is clear. But sunlight going down into the sea passes through more and more water. Each metre stops a little of the light. About 200 metres down, it is very dim. Below about 1,000 metres, there is no sunlight left, and the water is completely dark. Many animals live there, and lots of them make their own light.
examples: Water in a glass is clear.
In the milk test, half a glass of cloudy water let the coin show, but a full glass hid it.
Deep-sea fish such as anglerfish carry their own glowing lights.
explanations.context: This card says why the deep sea is dark.
explanations.art: A tall picture of the sea from the surface down: bright blue at the top, dimmer below, black at the bottom, with a glowing anglerfish deep down.

agreed.text: Some materials are transparent, some are translucent and some are opaque.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can hold glass, a napkin and a steel plate up to a window and see the difference.

agreed.text: More layers of a material let less light through.
agreed.evidence: In the Layer Test, the drawing got fainter with each square added. Light meters show the same thing very exactly.

agreed.text: Thin slices of most rocks let light through.
agreed.evidence: Since the 1850s, scientists have ground rocks into slices thinner than paper and looked at them with light shining through, under a microscope.

agreed.text: Below about 1,000 metres in the sea, no sunlight reaches.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have lowered light meters from ships and gone down in deep-sea vehicles, and measured the light fading away.

challenging.claim: Metal and rock can never let light through.
challenging.for: A coin, a bangle, a steel plate and a stone all block light completely.
challenging.against: Gold leaf, hammered very thin, lets green light through. Rock ground thinner than paper lets light through too. They block light only when they are thick.
challenging.context: This card is about metal and rock.

challenging.claim: If you cannot see through something, no light is getting through.
challenging.who: A common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: A thick pile of paper hides a drawing completely.
challenging.against: In the Layer Test, the pile that hid the drawing still glowed with a torch behind it. Light was getting through, but scattered, so there was no picture.
challenging.context: This card is about what hiding means.

challenging.claim: Clear water lets all the light through, however deep it is.
challenging.for: A glass of water, a bucket of water and the shallow sea at a beach all look clear.
challenging.against: The deep sea is completely dark below about 1,000 metres, because so much water above stops the sunlight. In the milk test, a full glass of cloudy water hid the coin, but half a glass let it show.
challenging.context: This card is about water and light.

big_questions.q: One tissue lets light through, and a whole roll of tissue does not. At which layer does the roll become opaque?
big_questions.hint: Did the light stop all at once in your test, or fade bit by bit? Is there one exact layer?

big_questions.q: When light runs out inside a pile of paper, where does it go?
big_questions.hint: Look at the front of the pile when the torch is behind it. Does some light come back towards the torch? Does the paper warm up a tiny bit?

big_questions.q: Your eyelids let in a red glow even when they are shut. Are you ever in complete darkness?
big_questions.hint: Try it in a bright room and in a dark room at night. When is there no glow at all?

big_questions.q: Fish deep in the sea live where sunlight never reaches. Is their world dark, or lit in a different way?
big_questions.hint: Many deep-sea animals make their own light. Who would you see if you went down there?

story.title: The Dosa That Let the Light In
story.note: Ajji means grandmother in Kannada and Tulu. Neer dosa is a very thin rice dosa from the coast of Karnataka. Mangaluru is a city by the sea in Karnataka. Nila, Varun, Amma and Ajji are made up.
text: Nila was seven. She lived on the sixth floor of a block of flats in Mangaluru, with her Amma and her Ajji. That week her cousin Varun was staying too. He was five, and he asked a question about everything.

It was a rainy Sunday in July. The rain drummed on the kitchen window. Ajji was making neer dosa for breakfast. Neer means water, and the batter was thin and white, like milk. Ajji poured it on to the hot pan and swirled it round. In a moment it set into a dosa so thin that it was full of tiny holes, like lace.
Ajji lifted the first dosa off the pan and put it on a steel plate. Nila picked it up by one edge and held it up to the window. "Look, Varun!" she said. "The light is coming through it."
The dosa glowed. Nila could see the bright square of the window behind it, but only as a pale patch. She could not see the rain or the coconut tree outside.
"It's see-through, like glass!" said Varun.
"Not quite," said Ajji, turning the next dosa. "Through glass, you can see the coconut tree. Can you see the tree through the dosa?"
Varun squinted. "No. Only light."
"Then the dosa is translucent," said Ajji. "It lets light through, but not a clear picture. The window glass is transparent. You see straight through it."
Ajji folded the dosa in half, and then in half again. Now it was four layers thick. Nila held it up to the window again. It still glowed, but it was much dimmer.
Varun ran to get his steel tumbler. He held it up to the window. "This one is dark!" he said. "No light at all."
"The steel is opaque," said Ajji. "It does not let light through."
By now there was a pile of folded dosas on the plate, six of them, one on top of another. Nila lifted the whole pile carefully and held it up. It was very dark. Almost no glow came through.
Nila frowned. "So is a dosa translucent, or opaque?"
"What do you think?" asked Ajji.

Nila thought about it. One dosa glowed brightly. Four layers glowed less. Six folded dosas, which made many layers, did not glow at all. "It depends how many there are," she said slowly. "Every layer stops some of the light. If there are enough layers, all the light is stopped."
Ajji smiled. "That is true for almost everything."
After breakfast the rain stopped, and the sun came out over the sea. From the balcony they could see the Arabian Sea, grey-blue and wide.

"When I was a girl," said Ajji, "I swam at Panambur beach. When I scooped the sea water up in my hands, it was as clear as tap water. But if I stood where the water came up to my chest, I could not see my own feet."
"Why not?" asked Varun.
"Think of the dosas," said Nila. "A little water is like one dosa. Lots of water is like the whole pile."

"Yes," said Ajji. "The sea also carries sand and tiny living things, which make it cloudy. Far out, where the sea is very deep, there is so much water above that no sunlight reaches the bottom at all. It is dark down there, all day and all night. Many fish and other animals there make their own light, to see and to be seen."
Varun's eyes went wide. "I want to see a fish with a light!"
That night, the power went off. Amma lit a small torch and gave it to Nila. Nila pulled her thin cotton bedsheet over her head and shone the torch. The sheet glowed all around her like a tent.
"Varun," she whispered, "this sheet is one layer. Get me the thick quilt."
Varun dragged the quilt over. Nila pulled it over the sheet. Now the glow was gone. It was dark and warm under there, like the bottom of the sea.
"Now we're deep-sea fish," said Varun, and switched on his own little light, which was the torch.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Nila works out that whether a dosa is translucent or opaque depends on how many layers there are. Each layer stops some of the light, and enough layers stop it all. Ajji then shows that the same is true of sea water: a handful is clear, but deep water is dark.
ask: Why could Nila see light through one dosa, but not the coconut tree?
What happened to the glow when Ajji folded the dosa into four layers?
Why could Ajji see the water in her hands clearly, but not her feet in the sea?
Under the bedsheet the torch glowed, but under the quilt it was dark. Why?
art: A grandmother at a stove in a flat kitchen pouring white batter into a pan, rain on the window, and a girl and a small boy watching.
A girl holding a lacy, thin dosa up to a rainy kitchen window, the dosa glowing white, and the boy holding up a dark steel tumbler.
A grandmother and two children on a high balcony, looking out at a wide grey-blue sea after rain, coconut trees below.
Two children under a glowing white bedsheet at night with a torch, and then under a thick quilt, only a small torch spot showing.

experiments.title: The Layer Test: how many layers hide the drawing?
experiments.context: In this experiment you pile squares of polythene, tissue and paper on a drawing, one at a time. You count how many layers it takes to hide the drawing. Then you shine a torch behind the pile to see if any light still gets through.
experiments.question: How many layers of clear polythene, tissue and white paper does it take to hide a drawing? When the drawing is hidden, does light still get through?
experiments.predict: Which material will hide the drawing with the fewest layers? Which will need the most? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same drawing, the same window light and squares of the same size every time. We add one layer at a time and look from the same place. We change only the material.
results_table: My guess: how many layers to hide the drawing?
How many layers it really took
With the torch behind that pile: glow or dark?

materials.item: a drawing card: a sun drawn with a thick black sketch pen or marker on white paper, about the size of a bottle cap
squares of clear polythene, each about the size of your palm, cut from clean, clear food bags or a carry bag
squares of tissue or paper napkin, the same size, one layer thick (pull two-layer tissues apart)
squares of plain white paper, the same size, from unruled notebook pages or old printer paper
a steel plate
a torch (a phone torch works too)
scissors (a grown-up cuts)
a pencil

experiments.safety: Don't shine the torch into anyone's eyes. Keep plastic bags and squares away from babies and toddlers.

schedule.what: Pile squares of three materials on a drawing, count the layers that hide it, then test each pile with a torch.

experiments.record: Fill in the table (a grown-up can write the words, and your child writes the numbers). Then draw a tower of squares for each material, as tall as the number of layers it took.

setup.art: A table by a window with a white card showing a thick black sun drawing, and three neat piles of squares: clear polythene, white tissue and white paper, plus a steel plate and a torch.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a thick sun. Cut ten squares of each material.

setup.art: A girl laying a white paper square flat on the sun drawing, two squares already on it, the sun showing faintly through.
setup.caption: 2. Add one square at a time. Can you still see the sun?

setup.art: The same girl writing the number 5 in a table beside a pile of paper squares, with the sun no longer visible.
setup.caption: 3. When the sun is gone, write down how many layers.

setup.art: A dim room, a phone torch lying on a table with its light pointing up under a pile of paper squares, and the pile glowing softly while a girl looks.
setup.caption: 4. Put the pile over the torch light. Does it glow?

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a sun with a thick black sketch pen on white paper. 2. You cut ten squares of each material. 3. Your child holds one square of each up to the window.
flow.say: Here are three materials: clear polythene, tissue and white paper. Hold one square of each up to the window. What do you see through each one?
flow.kid: Draw a big, thick sun. Hold one square of each up to the window. What can you see?
flow.parent: Never let your child look at the Sun itself, even through the squares. A window with daylight, or a bright tube light, is enough.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many layers of each material will hide the sun. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will pile squares on the sun, one at a time. How many layers of polythene will hide it? How many of tissue, and of paper? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many layers of each will hide the sun. Why?

ask.q: Why did you guess that the paper will need fewer layers than the polythene?
good: Paper is thicker.
I can see through polythene, but not really through paper.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write it down and don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Put the drawing on a table near the window. 2. Your child lays polythene squares on it one at a time, flat. 3. After each one, they look from where they sit. 4. Count the layers until the sun is gone. 5. Do the same with tissue, then paper. 6. Last, lay the steel plate on it.
flow.say: Lay one square flat on the sun. Can you still see it? Add another. Keep counting. Tell me the moment the sun is gone.
flow.kid: Add one square at a time. Count them. Stop when the sun is gone.

ask.q: What happened to the sun as you added paper squares?
good: It got fainter and fainter.
It went grey, then it was gone.

flow.parent: Paper usually hides a thick drawing in about 3 to 6 layers. Tissue often needs more, because each layer is thinner. The sun usually still shows through all 10 polythene squares, a little greyer. If a material still shows the sun at 10, write 'more than 10'. Your numbers may be different from these. What matters is what you see.

flow.do: 1. Draw the curtains or go to a dim room. 2. Lay the torch on the table with its light pointing up. A phone lies face down, with its torch pointing up. 3. Switch it on. 4. Lay the paper pile that hid the sun over the light, and look down at it. 5. Do the same with the tissue pile and the steel plate.
flow.say: This paper pile hid the sun completely. Now I put the torch behind it. Do you think any light will get through? Why?
flow.kid: The paper pile hid the sun. Will the torch glow through it?

good: Yes, it glowed.
Light came through, but I still can't see the sun.
No. It stayed dark.
Only the edges were bright, around the plate.

flow.parent: The paper and tissue piles glow, even though they hid the drawing. The steel plate gives no glow. If you have time, try a whole closed notebook over the torch. A thick notebook often stops the glow, or lets only a very faint glow through.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which material hid the sun with the fewest layers? The paper pile hid the sun, but did it stop all the light? What does each layer do to the light?
flow.kid: Which hid the sun fastest? Did the paper pile stop all the light? How do you know?

ask.q: What does each layer do to the light?
good: It stops a little bit.
Some light goes through, and some is stopped.

ask.q: Is the pile of paper translucent or opaque?
good: Translucent, because the torch glowed through it.
It hides the picture, but light gets through, so translucent.

check.q: Malini, a girl in Chennai, piles 5 paper squares on her drawing. The drawing is hidden. Then she shines a torch behind the pile. What will she see?
check.why: Each paper layer stops some light and lets the rest through. Five layers mix up the picture, but some light still comes out, so the pile glows.

experiments.title: The Milk Cloud: how many drops hide the coin?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop milk into a glass of clear water, a few drops at a time. You count the drops until you can no longer see a coin at the bottom. Then you take half the water out and look again.
experiments.question: How many drops of milk does it take to hide a coin at the bottom of a glass of water? If we take half the cloudy water out, can we see the coin again?
experiments.predict: How many drops do you think it will take to hide the coin? When we take half the water out, will the coin show again? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same glass, the same coin and the same window light. We stir the same way after every 5 drops. We always look straight down from the same height.

materials.item: a clear glass tumbler, or a clear plastic bottle with the top cut off by a grown-up
a second tumbler or steel glass, to hold the water you take out
a small steel katori or cup, to scoop water out
water, enough to fill the glass
a little milk in a katori or small bowl
a teaspoon, for dripping and stirring
a shiny coin
a torch, for the last step if there is time

schedule.what: Drip milk into water until a coin disappears, then take half out and look again.

experiments.record: Write how many drops it took. Draw the glass full, with the coin hidden, and half full, with the coin showing or not.

setup.art: A clear glass of water on a table by a window, a coin at the bottom, a katori of milk and a teaspoon beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Put a coin in a glass of water.

setup.art: A girl tilting a teaspoon of milk so that drops fall into the glass, and white clouds swirling in the water.
setup.caption: 2. Drip in 5 drops of milk. Stir. Look down at the coin.

setup.art: A girl looking straight down into a cloudy glass, unable to see the coin, and holding up fingers to count.
setup.caption: 3. Count the drops until the coin is gone.

setup.art: A parent scooping cloudy water out of the glass with a small steel katori into a steel tumbler, and the girl looking down into the half-full glass where the coin shows faintly.
setup.caption: 4. Scoop half the water out. Can you see the coin now?

flow.do: Fill the glass with water. Drop the coin in. Your child looks straight down at it.
flow.say: Look down into the glass. Can you see the coin? Is the water transparent?
flow.kid: Look down at the coin. Can you see it clearly?

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many drops of milk will hide the coin. Write it down.
flow.say: We will drip in milk, five drops at a time. How many drops will hide the coin? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many drops will hide the coin. Why?
flow.parent: Milk is mostly water, with tiny drops of fat and other tiny bits floating in it. These send light off in all directions.

flow.do: 1. Dip the teaspoon in the milk. 2. Tilt it over the glass so drops fall in. 3. Count 5 drops. 4. Stir and look. 5. Keep going in fives until the coin is gone.
flow.say: Five drops. Stir. Can you see the coin? Five more. Count them with me. Tell me when the coin is gone.
flow.kid: Count the drops in fives. Stir. Look down. Is the coin still there?

ask.q: What is happening to the water?
good: It is getting cloudy.
It is turning white, like weak milk.

flow.parent: The number of drops depends on your milk, your glass and your drops. It may be 20, or it may be 60. Keep counting in fives until the coin is really gone.

flow.do: Scoop about half the cloudy water into the other tumbler with the katori, so the coin stays put. Your child looks straight down into the half-full glass.
flow.say: The water is just as cloudy as before. But now there is only half as much. Will the coin show again? Why?
flow.kid: Now there is half as much water. Can you see the coin?

ask.q: Why can you see the coin again?
good: There is less water in the way.
Fewer layers of cloudy water.

flow.parent: Usually the coin shows again, faintly. If it doesn't, scoop out a little more. If you have time, shine a torch at the side of the glass in a dim room. The cloudy water glows, so light gets through it. It is translucent.

flow.do: Talk about the test.
flow.say: Clear water was transparent. With milk, it became cloudy. A full glass hid the coin, but half a glass did not. How is this like the Layer Test?
flow.kid: How is the cloudy water like the pile of paper?

check.q: Shreya, a girl in Pune, has a full glass of cloudy milky water. She cannot see the coin at the bottom. What can she do to see the coin, without adding anything?
options: Put the glass in a darker room
check.why: Less cloudy water means less of it in the way, so more light reaches the coin and comes back up. It is like taking squares off a pile.

activities.title: Three Plates: see through, glow or dark?
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You hold ten home things up to a window, one at a time. Then you put each one on a plate: see through, glow or dark.

materials.item: three steel plates, with a paper label on each: an eye for 'see through', a glow for 'glow', and a black circle for 'dark'

ten home things, for example: a glass tumbler, a clear plastic box, a paper napkin, a dry onion skin, a leaf from a potted plant, a thin cotton dupatta, a steel spoon, a wooden ladle, a coin and a coloured plastic file folder
a window with daylight, or a bright tube light

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun itself, even through something.

schedule.what: Hold ten things up to the light, and sort them on three plates.

activities.record: Draw the three plates and what you put on each.

setup.art: Three steel plates on the floor with labels: an eye, a soft glow and a black circle, and a basket of ten home things beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Label three plates. Gather ten things.

setup.art: A boy holding a dry onion skin up to a bright window, the skin glowing, with the window behind it only a blur.
setup.caption: 2. Hold each thing up to the window. Look through it.

setup.art: The three plates now filled: a glass and a clear box on the eye plate, a napkin, onion skin and dupatta on the glow plate, and a spoon, ladle and coin on the dark plate.
setup.caption: 3. Put each thing on the right plate.

flow.do: Show the three plates. Explain the labels.
flow.say: The eye plate is for things you can see straight through. The glow plate is for things that glow in the light, but you can't see through. The dark plate is for things that don't let light through.
flow.kid: Eye plate: see through. Glow plate: light only. Dark plate: no light.

flow.do: Your child holds each thing up to the window, says what they see, and puts it on a plate.
flow.say: Hold it up to the window. Can you see the window clearly? Does it glow? Which plate?
flow.kid: Hold it up. What do you see? Put it on a plate.

ask.q: Why did you put the onion skin on the glow plate?
good: Light came through, but I couldn't see the window.
It glowed.

flow.parent: The leaf and the onion skin usually glow. The coloured file folder may be clear enough to see through, or it may only glow. Let your child decide by looking.

flow.do: Look at the three plates together. Tell your child the three words.
flow.say: Things on the eye plate are called transparent. Things on the glow plate are called translucent. Things on the dark plate are called opaque. Which plate has the most things?
flow.kid: Eye plate: transparent. Glow plate: translucent. Dark plate: opaque.

check.q: Teju, a girl in Bengaluru, holds a paper napkin up to the window. It glows, but she cannot see the window through it. Which plate does it go on?
check.why: Light gets through the napkin, so it is not opaque. But there is no clear picture, so it is not transparent. It is translucent.

activities.title: Thin Slice, Thick Piece: the cucumber test
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up cuts a cucumber into a very thin slice, a thick slice and a big chunk. You hold each one up to the window and see which ones let light through.

materials.item: a cucumber
a knife and a chopping board, for a grown-up
an onion, if you have one
a window with daylight

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting.

schedule.what: Hold thin and thick pieces of cucumber up to the window.

activities.record: Draw the three pieces, and colour the ones that glowed.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a cucumber on a board into a paper-thin slice, a slice as thick as a finger and a big chunk.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts a thin slice, a thick slice and a chunk.

setup.art: A girl holding a paper-thin cucumber slice up to a window, glowing pale green, and a dark chunk in her other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Hold each one up to the window.

flow.do: Cut three pieces of cucumber. Make one slice as thin as you can. Make one slice as thick as a finger. Cut one chunk as long as your thumb.
flow.say: These three pieces are all cucumber. Which ones will let light through? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: All three are cucumber. Which will let light through? Why?

flow.do: Your child holds each piece up to the window.
flow.say: Hold up the thin slice. What do you see? Now the thick slice. Now the chunk.
flow.kid: Hold each piece up to the window. Which ones glow?

good: The thin slice glowed the most.
The thick slice glowed a little, and the chunk was dark.

flow.parent: If you have an onion, peel off one thin layer of the white part. Hold it up too, and then hold up the whole onion.

flow.do: Talk about it. Then eat the cucumber.
flow.say: Is cucumber translucent or opaque? Can it be both?
flow.kid: Is cucumber translucent or opaque? It depends on what?

good: How thick it was.
Thin pieces let light through, thick ones don't.

check.q: Gauri, a girl in Bhubaneswar, holds a very thin slice of potato up to the window. What will she most likely see?
check.why: A whole potato is opaque. But a very thin slice lets some light through, like the thin cucumber slice. So it glows a little.

games.title: Thin or Thick? A card game
games.players: 2 to 6 players. Take turns being the reader.
games.context: This is a card game. Each card names a thing. You say whether light goes straight through it, glows through it, or is stopped. Then you find the pairs: the thin and thick versions of the same material.

items.b: SEE THROUGH. A little water is transparent.

items.f: The deep sea, one kilometre down
items.b: DARK. So much water above stops all the sunlight.

items.f: A whole roll of toilet paper
items.b: DARK. Enough layers stop all the light.
GLOWS. A thin slice is translucent.
DARK. A thick piece is opaque.

items.f: Gold leaf, hammered much thinner than paper
items.b: GLOWS. Very thin gold lets green light through.

items.f: A slice of rock, ground thinner than paper
items.b: GLOWS. Most rocks let light through when they are this thin.
DARK. A thick rock is opaque.
SEE THROUGH. Window glass is transparent.

items.f: Your closed eyelids, facing a bright window
items.b: GLOWS. Eyelids are thin, so a warm red glow gets through.

rules: Mix the 12 cards and put them in a pile, face down.
The reader takes the top card and reads the front out loud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Everyone else shows an answer with their hands. Open hands wide means 'see through'. Wiggling fingers means 'glows'. Fists mean 'dark'. Everyone says why.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. Everyone who was right gets a point. Then the next player is the reader.

When all the cards are read, lay them face up. Find the five pairs: a thin thing and a thick thing made of the same material. Each pair you find is one more point. The window pane and the eyelids have no partner, so leave them out.
Add up the points. The most points wins. If you tie, you all win.

setup.art: Twelve cards in a pile on a mat, and a parent and two children sitting around them.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile, face down.

setup.art: Two children showing answers with their hands, one with open hands, one wiggling her fingers, while a parent reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. Show your answer with your hands. Then turn the card.

setup.art: The cards laid out face up in pairs: one glass of water next to the deep sea, a cucumber slice next to a whole cucumber.
setup.caption: 3. At the end, find the thin and thick pairs.

flow.do: Read the rules together. Practise the three hand signs. Decide who reads first.
flow.say: Open hands means see through. Wiggly fingers means glows. Fists mean dark. Let's try each one.
flow.kid: Open hands: see through. Wiggly fingers: glows. Fists: dark.

flow.do: Play all 12 cards. The reader reads each front, waits for every hand sign and reason, then reads the back. Pass the cards to the next reader.
flow.say: One paper napkin. Show me with your hands. Why did you choose that?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Show your answer with your hands.
flow.parent: The gold leaf and the rock slice are the surprises. If your child shows a fist, ask: what happened to the thin cucumber slice?

flow.do: Lay the cards face up and find the pairs together.
flow.say: Find a thin thing and a thick thing made of the same material. What is the same about every pair?
flow.kid: Find the pairs. What is the same in every pair?

check.q: Ishita, a girl in Kolkata, has two cards: 'one glass of water' and 'the deep sea'. Why is one see through and the other dark?
options: The deep sea has much more water in the way
Sea water is a different colour
There are fish in the way
check.why: Both are water. Each metre of water stops a little light. A glass holds very little, but the deep sea has so much water above that no sunlight reaches the bottom.

games.title: Window, Curtain, Wall: a moving game
games.players: 1 or more players, and a grown-up to call out. Take turns calling if you like.
games.context: This is a moving game. A grown-up calls out a thing. If light goes straight through it, you are a window. If it glows, you are a curtain. If it stops light, you are a wall.

items.f: A whole packet of paper napkins
A leaf held up to the sky
Your spectacles, or a pair of reading glasses

rules: Window: stand tall and make a square frame with your hands in front of your eyes, and look through it.
Curtain: sway gently from side to side, like a curtain in the breeze.
Wall: stand stiff and still, with your arms tight at your sides.
A grown-up calls out a thing. Everyone moves as fast as they can.
The grown-up says the answer. Anyone who chose differently says why. A good reason counts too.
When all 12 calls are done, count how many you moved right at the first try. Try to beat that next time.

setup.art: A girl making a square frame with her hands in front of her eyes, a boy swaying like a curtain, and a girl standing stiff like a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Learn the three moves: window, curtain, wall.

setup.art: A parent reading from a card, 'A thick quilt!', and three children all standing stiff like walls.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up calls a thing. Move fast!

flow.do: Show the three moves. Practise each one twice.
flow.say: Window: look through your hands. Curtain: sway. Wall: stand stiff. Let's try them.
flow.kid: Window: look through your hands. Curtain: sway. Wall: stand stiff.

flow.do: Call out all 12 things, in any order. After each call, say the answer. Keep count of the right moves.
flow.say: One paper napkin! Now: a whole packet of paper napkins! Why did you change?
flow.kid: Listen. Are you a window, a curtain or a wall?
flow.parent: The napkin and the packet of napkins are the key pair. One layer glows, many layers stop the light.

flow.do: Ask one last question.
flow.say: Which thing made you change from curtain to wall, just by adding more of it?
flow.kid: Which thing turned from curtain to wall when there was more of it?

check.q: Ammu, a girl in Thrissur, hears the call 'a thin cotton dupatta'. Which move should she make?
check.why: A thin dupatta lets light through, but you cannot see a clear picture through it. It is translucent, so she sways like a curtain.

projects.title: The Window Letter: a message only light can show
projects.context: In this project you write a secret message and hide it under layers of paper. On a table, nobody can read it. Held up to a bright window, the message appears.

materials.item: a sheet of white paper, from an unruled notebook or old printer paper
a thick black sketch pen or marker
two more sheets of the same white paper, and a third in case you need it
glue or tape
crayons or colour pencils

schedule.what: Write a message, hide it under paper layers, and test it at the window.

projects.record: Draw your letter on the table and at the window. Write how many layers you used.

setup.art: A girl writing 'HAPPY PONGAL PAATI' in big, thick black letters on white paper.
setup.caption: 1. Write a short message in big, thick letters.

setup.art: The girl gluing two more white sheets over the message, edge to edge, so the letters are hidden.
setup.caption: 2. Stick two sheets over it. Draw a picture on top.

setup.art: A parent holding the letter up to a bright window, and the dark letters of the message showing through clearly.
setup.caption: 3. Hold it up to a bright window. The message appears.

flow.do: Your child writes a short message in big, thick letters, pressing hard.
flow.say: Write a secret message for someone. Make the letters big and thick. Who will you give it to?
flow.kid: Write a short secret message. Use big, thick letters.

flow.do: 1. Lay one sheet over the message. 2. Look at it on the table. 3. Add the second sheet. 4. Look again. 5. When it can't be read on the table, glue the edges.
flow.say: Lay one sheet on top. Can you still read it? Add another. Can you read it now?
flow.kid: Add one sheet at a time. Stop when you can't read it.
flow.parent: One sheet often still shows the letters. Two sheets usually hide them on a table. If they still show, add a third sheet.

flow.do: Your child draws a picture on the top sheet with crayons, lightly, so it doesn't cover all of it.
flow.say: Draw a picture on top, so nobody guesses there is a message inside.
flow.kid: Draw a picture on top. Keep the message a secret.

flow.do: Hold the letter up to a bright window. Then give it to someone, and show them the trick.
flow.say: The paper hid your message on the table. Why can we read it at the window?
flow.kid: Hold it up to the window. What do you see? Why?

ask.q: Why does the message show at the window?
good: Light comes through the paper, but not through the black ink.
The paper is translucent, and the ink blocks light.

check.q: Vaishnavi, a girl in Madurai, covers her message with 2 sheets of paper. Her brother can still read it on the table. What should she do?
options: Add another layer of paper on top
Hold it closer to his eyes
check.why: Each layer hides the message a little more. One more layer will hide it on the table. It will still show at the window, because the paper is translucent.

challenges.title: The Nap Room: make a shoebox dark
challenges.context: This is a problem to solve. A shoebox room has a big window cut in its lid. You must make it dark inside, using as few layers as you can.
challenges.problem: Divya, a girl in Hyderabad, makes a shoebox room for her toy cat. It has a big window cut in the lid and a peephole at one end. The cat wants an afternoon nap. Divya must cover the window so the room is dark inside, even next to a bright window. She wants to use as few layers as she can.
constraints: Use only things you already have at home.
You must be able to lift the cover off again.
materials: a shoebox. A grown-up cuts a window in the lid, about the size of your palm, and a small peephole at one end
a small white paper cat or star, to stand inside the box
a thick cloth, such as a towel
general: Pile on sheets of newspaper until you can no longer see the white cat through the peephole.
Cover the window with one piece of cardboard.
creative: Use one piece of kitchen foil, which is opaque even when thin.
Make a flap that lifts. Two layers of paper on the flap give a soft glow for waking up. A thick towel on top makes it dark for the nap.
Fold the thick towel twice, so one towel makes four layers.
challenges.your_turn: Find two ways to make the room dark. Which used the fewest layers? Can you make a cover that gives a soft glow for waking up?

setup.art: A shoebox with a palm-sized window in its lid, a peephole at one end, and a white paper cat inside, next to a bright window.
setup.caption: 1. Look through the peephole. You can see the white cat.

setup.art: A girl laying newspaper sheets over the window in the lid and counting, then looking through the peephole.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the window. Count your layers. Look again.

flow.do: Set up the shoebox next to a bright window. Your child looks through the peephole. Read the problem.
flow.say: Can you see the white paper cat through the peephole? Now we must make the room dark, with as few layers as we can.
flow.kid: Look through the peephole. Can you see the cat? Now make it dark.

good: Lots of newspaper.
Something opaque, like foil or cardboard.

flow.do: Let your child try their ideas. Count the layers each time. Help only if asked.
flow.say: Try your idea. Count the layers. Look through the peephole. Can you still see the cat?
flow.kid: Try your idea. Count the layers. Can you still see the cat?

flow.do: Talk about which way worked best.
flow.say: Which cover used the fewest layers? Why did it need so few?
flow.kid: Which cover used the fewest layers? Why?

check.q: Divya needs 8 sheets of newspaper to make the box dark. Her friend Rahul uses only 1 layer. What might Rahul have used?
check.why: Cardboard is thick and opaque, so one layer stops the light. A napkin is translucent, and polythene is transparent.

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. Does light go straight through, glow through, or stop? Draw a line to the right box.
items.why: We see clearly through the glass and the polythene. The napkin and the onion skin glow, but show no clear picture. The plate and the door let no light through.

items.p: Remember the Layer Test, where you piled squares on a drawing of a sun. Which material still showed the sun after 10 layers?
items.why: Each polythene layer stops only a little light, so the sun still shows through many layers. Paper stops much more at each layer.

items.p: A pile of paper that hides a drawing stops all the light.
items.why: False. In the Layer Test, the paper pile hid the drawing, but it still glowed with a torch behind it. Some light got through.

items.p: Draw a torch shining on one paper square, and on a pile of five squares. Draw arrows of light coming out of each.
items.a: Many arrows come out of the one square. Only a few come out of the pile of five.
items.why: A strong drawing shows fewer arrows after more layers, because each layer stops some of the light.
items.art: An empty box with a small torch drawn on each side, pointing up.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: You can see clearly through it
Light gets through, but no clear picture
items.why: These are the three ways a material can treat light.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: the paper pile hid your drawing, but the torch glowed through it. Is the pile translucent or opaque? How do you know?
items.a: Translucent, because light from the torch came through it, even though I could not see the drawing.
items.why: A strong answer uses the glow as the evidence: opaque things give no glow at all.

items.p: Each layer of paper stops some of the ____.
items.why: Each layer stops some light and lets the rest go on. So more layers let less light through.

items.p: Nila, aged 7, and her cousin Varun, aged 5, hold neer dosas up to the kitchen window in Mangaluru.

views.says: A dosa is see-through, because I can see light through it.
A dosa is not see-through, because a big pile of dosas is dark.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own tests. Then say what the other person noticed that is true.
items.a: Both are partly right. One dosa is translucent: light gets through, but no clear picture. A thick pile of dosas is opaque.
items.why: A strong answer says it depends on how many layers there are, and uses evidence such as the paper squares or the cucumber slices. It is fair to both: Varun really did see light, and Nila really saw the pile go dark.

items.p: Look at this room. Count only the things that are transparent. Write the number.
items.why: There are 3 transparent things: the window glass, the glass of water and the clear plastic box. The curtain is translucent. The almirah, the door and the steel plate are opaque.
items.art: A room with a glass window, a thin curtain beside it, a glass of water on a table, a clear plastic box, a steel almirah, a wooden door and a steel plate.

items.p: Three of these let some light through. Which one is opaque? Circle it.
items.why: A steel spoon lets no light through, so it is opaque. The napkin and the leaf glow, and a glass bangle lets light through.

items.p: In the Milk Cloud test, you took half the cloudy water out, and the coin showed again. Why? Say it, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: There was less cloudy water in the way, so more light got down to the coin and back up to my eyes.
items.why: A strong answer says the water was just as cloudy, but there was less of it, like taking squares off a pile.

items.p: Here are some Layer Test results: paper hid the sun at 4 layers, tissue at 8, and polythene still showed it at 10. Put the materials in order, from the one that stops the most light at each layer to the one that stops the least.
items.why: Paper needed the fewest layers, so each paper layer stops the most light. Polythene stops the least, because the sun still showed after 10.

items.p: Look at the picture of a bathroom. Write T for transparent, L for translucent or O for opaque on each thing.
items.why: We see straight through the tumbler. The frosted window lets light in but shows no view. The door lets no light through.
items.art: A bathroom with a clear glass tumbler on a shelf, a glowing frosted window and a wooden door, each with an empty label.

items.p: A slice of rock ground thinner than paper can let light through.
items.why: True. Scientists grind rocks into very thin slices, and most of them then let light through. This is how they study rocks under a microscope.

items.p: Draw the sea from the top to the bottom. Colour it bright at the top, dimmer in the middle and dark at the bottom. Draw one animal at the bottom, with the light she makes.
items.a: Bright at the top, dim in the middle, black at the bottom, with a glowing animal deep down.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the light fading little by little with depth, not stopping all at once.
items.art: A tall, empty box with a wavy line at the top for the surface of the sea.

items.p: Will each one glow, or look dark, when held up to a bright window?
items.why: Thin things let some light through and glow. Thick things, or many layers, stop the light and look dark.

items.p: Anjali and her friend Fathima, both aged 7, argue about paper in Kochi.

views.says: Paper is translucent. One sheet glows at the window.
Paper is opaque. My thick notebook is dark at the window.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use your Layer Test to give a reason. Then say what the other girl got right.
items.a: Both are right about what they saw. One sheet of paper is translucent. Enough sheets, like a thick notebook, can be opaque.
items.why: A strong answer says the answer depends on how thick the paper is, and uses evidence from the Layer Test. It is fair to both girls.

items.p: A bathroom window is made of frosted glass. What does it do?
opts: Lets light in, but no clear view
items.why: Frosted glass scatters the light that goes through it. The room gets daylight, but you cannot see a clear picture of outside.

items.p: One sheet of paper and a thick closed notebook are both translucent.
items.why: False. One sheet glows, so it is translucent. A thick notebook has so many sheets that it can stop nearly all the light.

items.p: You close your eyes and face a bright window. What do you see?
opts: A clear picture of the window
items.why: Your eyelids are thin, so some light gets through them. It is a glow, not a picture.

items.p: Polythene still showed the sun after 10 layers. Do you think it would still show it after 50 layers? Why? How could you find out?
items.a: Probably not clearly. Each layer stops a little light, so after enough layers the sun would get faint and then hidden. I could pile on 50 squares and look.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that each layer stops some light, and suggests a real test instead of just guessing.

items.p: Two scientists look at a gold bangle and at gold leaf, which is gold hammered much thinner than paper.

views.says: Gold is opaque. A gold bangle lets no light through.
Gold is not always opaque. Gold leaf lets green light through.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say how both could be right.
items.a: Both are right. Thick gold is opaque. Very thin gold lets some light through. It depends on thickness.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same material can stop light or let some through, depending on how thick the piece is.

items.p: Suresh did the Layer Test, but his very first tissue square hid the sun. What is the most likely reason?
opts: His sun was drawn too faintly in pencil
items.why: One tissue layer normally lets a thick drawing show. A faint pencil drawing is hidden much more easily. Using a thick black sketch pen makes the test fair.

items.p: Lalitha's baby brother naps in the afternoon. The window has a thin curtain, and the room is too bright. Write two ways to make the room dimmer, using what you learned about layers.
items.a: Hang a second curtain behind the first one. Or use a thicker cloth, or fold the curtain double.
items.why: A strong answer uses more layers or a thicker material, because each layer stops more light.

items.p: Draw light going down into the sea, with arrows. Draw many arrows at the top, fewer in the middle and none at the bottom.
items.a: Many arrows at the surface, fewer lower down, and none at the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that each layer of water stops some light, so the arrows run out with depth.
items.art: A tall, empty box with a Sun drawn above it.

items.p: When Ritu presses a torch to the back of a pile of 5 paper squares, the front glows. What does the glow tell her?
opts: Some light is getting through the pile
The paper makes its own light
items.why: Paper makes no light of its own. The glow is torch light that got through all five layers. So the pile is translucent, not opaque.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that lets the most light through to the one that lets the least.
items.why: Each napkin stops some light, so more napkins let less light through.

items.p: A thick enough piece of any material stops nearly all the light.
items.why: True. Each layer stops some light, so enough thickness stops almost all of it, even for glass or water.

items.p: Why are blackout curtains made with thick or double layers?
items.why: Each layer stops some light, so thick or double curtains keep a bedroom dark in the day.

items.p: Light that comes out of a pile of translucent paper is a glow, not a clear ____.
items.why: The layers scatter the light, so the picture gets mixed up, but some light still comes out.

quiz.why: We can see clearly through glass. A napkin only glows, and a door lets no light through.

quiz.p: Which word means that light gets through, but you see no clear picture?
quiz.why: Translucent means light gets through, but no clear picture. Transparent means you see clearly through it. Opaque means no light gets through.
A steel plate lets no light through. The box is transparent, and the dupatta is translucent.
An onion skin lets light through but shows no clear picture. Glass is transparent, and a steel spoon is opaque.

quiz.p: In the Layer Test, what happened to the drawing as more paper squares were added?
opts: It got fainter and then disappeared
quiz.why: Each layer stops some light, so the drawing faded with every square until it was gone.

quiz.p: To make the Layer Test fair, what do we change?
quiz.why: In a fair test we change only one thing. Then we know the material made the difference.

quiz.p: A pile of paper hides a drawing. A torch behind the pile makes it glow. What does that show?
opts: Light still gets through the pile
quiz.why: The glow is torch light that got through. So the pile hides the picture but is still translucent.

quiz.p: A whole cucumber is opaque. What about a paper-thin slice of it?
quiz.why: A thin slice glows at the window. It is translucent, because it is thin.

quiz.p: What happens when gold is hammered thinner than paper into gold leaf?
opts: It lets some green light through
quiz.why: Thick gold is opaque, but very thin gold leaf lets a little green light through.

quiz.p: Why is it completely dark deep in the sea?
opts: So much water above stops all the sunlight
Sea water at the bottom is black
The Sun does not shine on the sea
quiz.why: Each metre of water stops a little light. Below about 1,000 metres, no sunlight is left.

quiz.p: In the Milk Cloud test, which glass let the coin show again?
quiz.why: With less cloudy water in the way, more light reached the coin and came back.

videos.check: Found by search: "The Art of Gold Beating (1959) | British Pathé" by British Pathé, 3 minutes 16 seconds. A parent may preview it.

applications: Curtain makers sell thick or double-layered curtains, called blackout curtains, to keep a bedroom dark in the day.
Scientists who study rocks grind them into slices thinner than paper, so light can shine through and they can study the rock under a microscope.
A pulse oximeter, the small clip a doctor puts on your finger, shines light through your fingertip. The light that gets through tells it how much oxygen your blood carries.
Paper lanterns and lamp shades use thin paper or cloth, so the light glows through softly.
Seaweeds and corals that need sunlight live in the upper part of the sea, where enough light still reaches.

spotted.text: In Ahmedabad at Uttarayan, kites made of thin paper glow in the sunlight as they fly.
spotted.art: A blue sky full of colourful paper kites over the rooftops of Ahmedabad, with the sun shining through one bright kite.

spotted.text: At a Kerala sadya, hold your banana leaf up to the sky before the food comes. The thin leaf glows green.
spotted.art: A child holding a banana leaf up to the sky, the leaf glowing green with its lines showing.

spotted.text: At night in Kolkata during Durga Puja, the cloth walls of a pandal glow from the lights inside.
spotted.art: A big cloth pandal at night, glowing yellow from the lights inside, with crowds outside.

spotted.text: At Kovalam beach, the water near your feet is clear, but far out the sea looks dark blue.
spotted.art: A beach with clear, shallow water near the sand and deep blue sea far out, with a lighthouse on the hill.

spotted.text: In a flat in Guwahati, a thin cotton curtain lets in soft light, but a thick bedsheet hung behind it makes the room dark for an afternoon nap.
spotted.art: A bedroom window with a thin curtain glowing, and a thick bedsheet hung half across it, darkening part of the room.

open_questions.q: How little light can deep-sea animals see?
open_questions.why_open: Below about 1,000 metres, sunlight is too faint for most eyes. But some deep-sea fish have very sensitive eyes. Scientists are still finding out how faint a light they can sense.

open_questions.q: Could wood be made see-through and used for windows?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made thin wood that lets light through, by taking out part of the wood and filling it with clear plastic. Nobody knows yet if it can be made cheap and strong enough to replace glass in homes.

open_questions.q: Is there anything that no thickness can stop?
open_questions.why_open: Tiny particles called neutrinos pass right through the whole Earth, almost always without being stopped. Scientists are still finding out what neutrinos are like, for example exactly how heavy they are.

ask_kids: Which things in this room are transparent? Which are translucent?

maths.problem: In the Layer Test, Harini's paper hid the sun at 4 layers. Her tissue hid it at 9 layers. How many more tissue layers did she need?
maths.explain: Count on from 4 to 9: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. That is 5. So tissue needed 5 more layers than paper.
maths.context: This is about the Layer Test, where you counted the layers that hid a drawing.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how much more light each paper layer stops than each tissue layer.

maths.problem: Here are Sneha's results. Paper hid the sun at 5 layers, tissue at 8, and a steel plate at 1. Put them in order, from fewest layers to most.
maths.explain: 1 is the smallest, then 5, then 8. So the order is steel plate, paper, tissue.
maths.context: This is about the Layer Test, with made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Putting the results in order shows at a glance which material stops the most light at each layer.

maths.problem: Nila, a girl of 7, folds a paper napkin in half. Now it is 2 layers. She folds it in half again: 4 layers. Again: 8 layers. How many layers after one more fold?
maths.explain: Each fold doubles the layers: 2, 4, 8, then 8 and 8 more, which is 16.
maths.context: This is about folding a napkin to make more layers.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the doubling pattern tells you how quickly folding piles up layers, and so how quickly it stops the light.

maths.problem: In the Milk Cloud test, Revathi added milk 5 drops at a time. The coin disappeared after she had done this 6 times. How many drops did she add?
maths.explain: 6 groups of 5 drops: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. So she added 30 drops.
maths.context: This is about the Milk Cloud test, where you dripped milk into water.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups is a quick way to count many drops without losing track.

maths.problem: Asha did the Layer Test twice with paper. The first time the sun was hidden at 4 layers. The second time it was hidden at 2 layers, because it had gone cloudy outside. Which result would you trust, and what would you do?
maths.answer: Do both tests in the same light, and test again.
maths.explain: With less light, the drawing is harder to see, so it seems to hide sooner. The light changed, so the test was not fair. Test again in the same light and see if the numbers match.
maths.context: This is about the Layer Test, and two results that did not match.
maths.why_maths: When two numbers from the same test don't match, it is a clue that something else changed.

warmup.q: What do we call a material we can see clearly through?
A napkin glows at the window. Is it transparent, translucent or opaque?
Is a steel plate transparent, translucent or opaque?
Do more layers let more light through, or less?
Can a pile of paper hide a picture and still glow?
Why is the deep sea dark?
warmup.a: So much water above stops all the sunlight.

roots.context: We have piled up squares until a drawing disappeared, and watched a torch glow through the pile. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: One sheet of paper over your drawing still let you see it. A few more sheets hid it, but the torch still glowed through them. Each sheet stops some of the light and lets the rest pass on. So whether paper is translucent or opaque depends on how many sheets there are.
deep_truth.habit: We sort materials into fixed groups, as if paper is always translucent and rock is always opaque. But the group depends on the piece: one sheet of paper glows, a thick notebook can be dark, and rock ground thinner than paper lets light through.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Layer Test, the drawing faded with every paper square until it was gone, yet the pile still glowed with a torch behind it. A thin cucumber slice glowed at the window, but a thick chunk was dark.

three.who_am_i: Your eyelids are thin layers of skin. Facing a bright window with your eyes shut, you still see a warm glow, because some light gets through them.
three.what_is_life: Seaweeds and corals that need sunlight live near the top of the sea, where the water above is thin enough to let light through. Deep down, many animals make their own light.
three.what_is_this_world: Light meets everything, and everything lets through a little or a lot of it. Whether light gets through depends on what a thing is made of and how thick it is.

roots.thread: One torch sends out light. Each layer it meets takes a share of the light and passes on the rest. So the light fades little by little, until there is none left to pass on. Paper, water, a leaf and a rock all meet the same light, each in its own measure. Everything is aware in its own way, the paper and the water too. Many scientists disagree, and say only living beings with nerves are aware.

teachings.teaching: As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror is covered by dust, and as a baby is covered by the womb, so wisdom is covered by desire.
teachings.link: The Gita gives three coverings, from thin to thick. Smoke dims a fire, but its light still shows. Dust hides a mirror's picture. The womb hides the baby completely. In your Layer Test, too, each layer covered a little more.

teachings.teaching: Jain thinkers teach that every soul can know all things, but kinds of karma cover that knowledge. The first kind they name is jnanavaraniya, which means 'knowledge-covering'. As the covering thins, more knowledge shines through.
teachings.link: In your Layer Test, taking squares off the pile let more light through. The Jain teaching uses the same picture of layers for how much we can know.

science.text: Each layer of a material stops some of the light that reaches it, so light fades bit by bit through thicker pieces. Below about 1,000 metres, the sea has no sunlight at all.
Most rocks let light through when they are ground thinner than paper, and very thin gold leaf lets green light through.

other_view.who: The Buddha, in the Phena Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 22.95)
other_view.view: The Buddha compared what we call a self to the trunk of a banana plant. Someone cuts it open looking for a hard core and peels away layer after layer, but finds no core inside. In this view, there is no hidden self under the layers waiting to shine through. There are only the layers.

practice.title: Light through your eyelids
practice.say: Sit facing a bright window, but never look at the Sun. Close your eyes gently. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly, three times. What colour do you see with your eyes shut? Now cup your hands over your closed eyes. What happened to the glow? Take your hands away slowly. Where does the glow come from?
practice.kid: Sit facing a bright window. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. What colour do you see? Now cup your hands over your eyes. Is the glow still there? Take your hands away slowly.

ask: Your eyelids let light in even when they are shut. Is the glow you see inside you, or outside you?
The light faded layer by layer in your test. Was there ever one moment when it stopped?
If everything lets through a little light when it is thin enough, is anything truly opaque?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged facing a bright window with eyes closed, a soft red-orange glow drawn over the closed eyes, and a small pile of paper squares on the floor beside them.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought rocks were simply opaque. Light could not get through them, so the only way to study a rock was to look at its outside. In the 1830s, William Nicol in Scotland found a way to grind fossil wood so thin that light shone through it. Around 1850, Henry Clifton Sorby, a scientist in Sheffield, England, did the same with rocks. He glued a chip of rock to glass and ground it down until it was thinner than paper. Held up to the light, most of the rock was not opaque at all. It glowed, and under a microscope he could see the tiny grains inside it. His method spread. In the 1890s, Florence Bascom, one of the first women geologists in the USA, became an expert at reading rock slices like these. Geologists all over the world, in India too, still study thin rock slices today.
how_we_found_out.who: William Nicol, a Scottish scientist; Henry Clifton Sorby, an English scientist; Florence Bascom, an American geologist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a rock could only be studied from the outside, because rock is opaque. Sorby ground rocks thinner than paper and showed that most of them let light through.

founder: ideas/by_topic/light-seeing-and-shadows.md: the founder's idea of shining a torch through different plastics and layered transparent sheets grew into the Three Plates sort and the Layer Test. Her note on C.V. Raman and light passing through transparent materials is kept for the Level 3 light units, since the colour of the sea is already told at Level 1.

Curriculum entry sci.light.transparent-opaque.L2 (covers: which materials let light through), with Cambridge Primary Science Stage 2 Unit 5, where children count sheets of paper in front of a torch. This unit leads on from Light sources (Level 2) and leads to Transparent, translucent and opaque (Level 3), which explains scattering and the gap test.
science: Light is attenuated exponentially with thickness in an absorbing or scattering medium (the Beer-Lambert law for absorption). In clear ocean water, the sunlit zone reaches about 200 metres and essentially no sunlight remains below about 1,000 metres.

Thin sections for petrography are ground to about 0.03 mm. William Nicol made thin sections of fossil wood around 1830. Henry Clifton Sorby applied the method to rocks from about 1849 and published 'On the microscopical structure of crystals' in 1858.

Florence Bascom (1862 to 1945) earned a PhD at Johns Hopkins in 1893 on old volcanic rocks of South Mountain, Pennsylvania, studied in thin section, and became the first woman geologist hired by the US Geological Survey in 1896.
Michael Faraday, Bakerian Lecture 1857, 'Experimental Relations of Gold (and other Metals) to Light': thin gold leaf transmits green light.
Milk is about 87 percent water. Its fat globules and casein micelles scatter light, which makes it white and opaque.
Pulse oximeters measure the red and infrared light transmitted through a fingertip.
Transparent wood: lignin removed and replaced with a clear polymer (Li and colleagues, KTH, 2016; Zhu and colleagues, University of Maryland, 2016).

Bhagavad Gita 3.38: dhumenavriyate vahnir yathadarsho malena cha, yatholbenavrito garbhas tatha tenedam avritam. Tattvartha Sutra chapter 8 (sutra 4 or 5, by edition) lists the eight kinds of karma, beginning with jnanavarana. Samyutta Nikaya 22.95 (Phena Sutta): form like foam, feeling like a bubble, perception like a mirage, fabrications like a banana trunk with no heartwood, consciousness like a magic trick.
